before: Maybe you've let a small child win at Go Fish and never found a good time to start playing for real. Who wants to be the grown-up who finally wins? Without the Guide, you can slide from looking after your little one into spoiling it the same way. Sweets and screens can pass for loving yourself, and so can getting it out of anything hard.
after: Once a need does show, after all that hiding, it's okay to want a lot of closeness. Then someone you love goes for a walk alone, and you've sent "hello??" before they've reached the corner. Look at how you're going about getting the need met, since demanding instant replies, or making someone pay for needing space, is another matter. The Guide helps you find a way that works for you both. But give the need a fair hearing first: I think your little one wants to know they're coming back.

guide_passage:
The r4 guide's passage (the passage this carries):
The opposite trap is forced adulthood: perfect discipline, no visible needs, and very little joy or closeness. In that case the next adult act may be asking for help, expressing a preference, or letting a safe person see something imperfect—not tightening control again.
brief:
- the meaning, in plain words: the opposite trap is forced adulthood: holding yourself to perfect discipline, never letting a need show, and very little joy or closeness. If you're stuck there, the next grown-up step may be asking someone safe for help, or saying what you'd like, not tightening your grip again.
- show the trap before you name it: one person's ordinary week (the reader's: "you", or "maybe you're the one who..."), with details that each carry one of its signs: discipline kept perfect, a need nobody gets to see, not much joy or closeness. Then name it in a short plain sentence (forced adulthood, the opposite of the trap in P2). No definition with a colon or a "where" clause.
- give the next grown-up step as something the reader could actually do this week: asking someone safe for help with something specific, or saying what you'd like about something specific. One "may" or "might" is enough, since it's one way out, not a rule. Say the urge to tighten your grip again plainly, as what the reader will probably want to do instead.
- the article's voice can give an opinion ("I'd...", "I think..."), ask a question, or react in a few words. Never a memory or experience of the author's own life.
- context, not for the text: in this round, what read Human in Pangram were a specific moment with an odd, exact detail ("you've sent "hello??" before they've reached the corner"), a question ("Who wants to be the grown-up who finally wins?"), and an opinion ("I think your little one wants to know they're coming back."). What read AI, even after a good scene, was the guide's content said the guide's way, in the guide's order: "That's the opposite trap, forced adulthood, where you hold yourself to perfect discipline and never let a need show. There's very little joy or closeness in it. If you're stuck there, the next grown-up step may be asking someone safe for help, or saying what you'd like."
- context, not for the text: don't use "If you're stuck there", "very little joy or closeness", "No wonder", or the two options in one "may be X, or Y" sentence. Already tried, and read AI: doing the dishes at a party, eating standing up at the counter. When to Change the Strategy already has "texting a friend that you're having a rough day instead of saying you're fine", so not that or anything like it. P2 just used a child's card game; don't use another game.
